title: Why Am I Getting This Feedback?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Team members who have received feedback meant to belittle them become suspicious of all feedback that follows, questioning whether each new critique is meant to help or harm. The familiar praise-first sandwich doesn't solve this—it trains recipients to discount the praise as camouflage, reinforcing their suspicion. Research on 'Stretch Feedback' (from Admired Leadership, drawing on David Yeager's developmental psychology) shows a more effective approach: pairing honest, high standards with explicit confidence in the person's capacity to meet them. This removes the doubt about the critic's motive and replaces defensiveness with motivation. The approach only works when the standards are real, the feedback is specific and actionable, and the leader genuinely believes in the person.
points: Team members who've experienced weaponized feedback start interrogating every subsequent critique—and that suspicion suppresses their motivation to improve.
The praise-criticism sandwich backfires: it teaches recipients to discount praise as cover for criticism, which only deepens the suspicion it was meant to defuse.
Stretch Feedback pairs honest standards with explicit confidence: 'This isn't ready yet, and I'm holding you to a high bar because I know you can meet it.'
David Yeager's research shows this combination works because it removes the doubt about whether the critic believes the receiver is capable—which is often the real obstacle.
The approach requires sincerity: the standards must be genuine, the feedback specific and actionable, and the leader must actually believe in the person's potential.
quotes: This uncertainty raises hard questions: Is this feedback meant to put me in my place or help me to get better? Does the leader believe I am capable of improving, or is this criticism designed to showcase my incompetence?

Many leaders have been taught to surround criticism with general praise (the familiar feedback sandwich), but that comes with a hidden cost. It teaches people to discount the praise as cover for the criticism, which only confirms the suspicion leaders are trying to defuse in the first place.
Stretch Feedback is more direct. Rather than softening the criticism to make it easier to hear, it combines honesty with a belief in the person’s potential.

His core idea is that by communicating both high standards and confidence in the student’s ability to meet them, the feedback removes the doubt many kids feel about why the criticism was offered — and whether the teacher believes they are up to the challenge.
When teachers and mentors communicate that they believe students can do hard things, young people are motivated to meet those expectations.
The good news is that leaders don’t need a psychology degree to put this into practice.
